nameStory: The Chinese angelica-tree gets its name from its native home in China and its resemblance to true angelica plants, which were once thought to have angelic healing powers. The 'tree' part is a bit misleading since it's more of a large shrub or small tree, but early botanists were impressed enough by its towering compound leaves to give it tree status in the name.
description: Chinese angelica-tree is a striking deciduous shrub or small tree that can reach 15-20 feet tall. It's famous for its enormous, twice-compound leaves that can stretch 3-4 feet long, giving it an almost tropical appearance despite being cold-hardy. In late summer, it produces large, showy clusters of small white flowers followed by dark purple berries. This Asian native is occasionally planted as an ornamental and rarely escapes cultivation in New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Massive twice-compound leaves up to 4 feet long with dozens of oval leaflets arranged along branching stems. The leaflets feel smooth and papery, with finely toothed edges that are slightly rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, frothy clusters of tiny creamy-white flowers appear in late summer, forming umbrella-like sprays at the branch tips that can be 1-2 feet across and smell faintly sweet.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small dark purple to black berries in large drooping clusters, each berry about the size of a peppercorn with a slightly wrinkled texture when ripe.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a multi-stemmed shrub or single-trunked small tree with an open, umbrella-like crown and relatively few thick branches that give it an architectural look.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish-brown bark on young stems that becomes slightly furrowed with age, and stems that feel sturdy but lightweight when broken.

habitat: Rarely found in New England, this plant occasionally appears in parks, botanical gardens, or around old homesteads where it was planted as an ornamental. When it does escape cultivation, it prefers rich, well-drained soils in partially shaded areas. You're most likely to spot it in urban or suburban settings rather than deep in natural forests.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in spring, unfurling from large buds to create an impressive tropical-looking display as the massive compound leaves expand.
seasonality.summer: The enormous leaves are at their peak, and distinctive umbrella-like flower clusters appear in late summer, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-brown before dropping, and dark purple berry clusters become prominent and persist into early winter.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the distinctive architectural branching pattern, and thick buds at branch tips hint at the massive leaves to come.

funFact: Despite being called a tree, Chinese angelica-tree can grow leaves so enormous that a single leaf can be taller than a person and contain over 100 individual leaflets - making it one of the most leaf-heavy plants you'll ever encounter!
confusionNotes: The massive twice-compound leaves are so distinctive that it's hard to confuse this with anything else in New England. The only similar plants would be other Aralia species like devil's walkingstick, but that species has thorny stems while Chinese angelica-tree is thornless.
contextualKnowledge: This is actually one of the rarest plants you could encounter in wild New England, with only 2 recorded observations. Most of the Aralia family members you'll find here are much smaller woodland herbs, making this tree-sized relative quite the anomaly.
compareHints: Unlike its native New England Aralia cousins which are mostly low woodland herbs, Chinese angelica-tree grows much larger and lacks the thorns found on devil's walkingstick. It's also much less common than American spikenard or wild sarsaparilla, and its leaves dwarf those of any native Aralia species. The flower clusters are also positioned at branch tips rather than arising from the leaf bases like in most native species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild sarsaparilla is much shorter than its Aralia relatives - bristly sarsaparilla grows taller with prickly stems, while American spikenard can reach 6 feet with multiple compound leaves and a more robust appearance.

Among New England's Aralia species, bristly sarsaparilla is the shortest and most rough-textured, preferring dry soils unlike wild sarsaparilla's forest preference or American spikenard's love of rich, moist areas.

American spikenard is much larger and more robust than its relatives - wild sarsaparilla stays close to the ground with leaves only 6-12 inches tall, while bristly sarsaparilla is covered in prickles.

Among its Aralia relatives in New England, Japanese angelica tree is by far the tallest and most tree-like, while wild sarsaparilla stays low to the ground and American spikenard is an herbaceous perennial.
Among its Aralia relatives in New England, devil's walkingstick is unmistakable due to its woody, tree-like growth and extensive spines.
Japanese spikenard dwarfs its New England relatives like wild sarsaparilla and American spikenard, growing 2-3 times taller with much more robust stems.
